resources.string: Why does soap clean grease when water won’t?
Oil floats on water and won’t mix in. Add soap, then shake.
Soap dissolves the oil away
Soap makes the water warmer
Soap wraps the oil so water can carry it
Soap doesn’t destroy grease. It packages it so water can carry it away.

A soap molecule has two ends: one that clings to water, one that clings to oil. The oil-loving ends bury themselves in a grease droplet while the water-loving ends face outward, forming a tiny ball — a micelle. The grease is now wrapped in a water-friendly shell, and it rinses straight off.
POLARITY • INTERMOLECULAR FORCES • SURFACTANTS
Surfactant + oil + H₂O → oil-in-water micelle
Why does a cut apple turn brown?
Slice an apple. Brush one half with lemon juice and wait.
The air dries the surface out
Oxygen reacts with the apple’s own chemicals
Bacteria settle on the cut face
Cutting the apple lets oxygen reach enzymes that turn its phenolic compounds into brown pigments.

An intact apple keeps polyphenol oxidase and many phenolic compounds separated inside its cells. Cutting breaks those compartments and exposes them to oxygen. The enzyme then helps oxidise the phenols, producing compounds that polymerise into brown pigments. Lemon juice slows this by lowering the pH and by supplying ascorbic acid, an antioxidant.
ENZYMES • OXIDATION • CATALYSIS
Phenolics + O₂ → o-quinones → melanin (browning)
Why does bread turn brown in a toaster?
Drop bread over the hot wires. Cover one corner with foil.
The bread is starting to burn
The heat simply dries the surface
Heat makes its sugars and proteins react together
Heat drives the bread’s sugars and proteins into hundreds of new brown, savoury molecules.

This is the Maillard reaction — the same family of browning reactions behind seared meat, roasted coffee and fried onions. As a dry surface gets hot, reducing sugars react with amino groups from proteins and create a complex mixture of new aromatic and brown compounds. Push the heating much further and true charring begins.
MAILLARD REACTION • THERMAL CHEMISTRY • AMINO ACIDS
Reducing sugar + amino acid + heat → melanoidins (Maillard browning)
Why does a fizzy drink fizz the moment you open it?
A sealed bottle sits perfectly still. Take the cap off.
The drop in pressure lets dissolved gas escape
Air rushes in and bubbles back up
Opening the bottle warms the drink
The cap was holding carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure. Release the pressure and it leaves.

Fizzy drinks are bottled with carbon dioxide forced into the liquid under pressure — far more than it could normally hold. Sealed, it stays dissolved. Open the cap and the pressure above the liquid falls to normal, so the gas is no longer forced to stay in solution. It comes out as bubbles, starting wherever it can get a grip: a scratch, a speck of dust, the wall of the glass.
SOLUBILITY • PRESSURE • HENRY’S LAW
CO₂(aq) ⇌ CO₂(g)↑ + H₂O (as pressure drops)
Why does a cold can get wet on the outside?
Take a cold can into a warm room and watch its surface.
The can is leaking a little
Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold metal
The cold soaks straight through the aluminium
The cold can cools nearby air below its dew point, so invisible water vapour condenses into liquid droplets.

Air always holds some water as an invisible gas, and warm air holds more of it. When that air touches the chilled metal it cools past the point where it can keep all that water as vapour, and the excess condenses onto the surface as droplets. The water was in the room the whole time — the cold can just gave it somewhere to gather.
CONDENSATION • DEW POINT • PHASE CHANGE
H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) (below dew point)
Why does salt melt ice on a winter road?
Scatter salt on an ice cube and watch a thermometer beside it.
Salt is warm and thaws the ice
Salt is heavy and crushes the ice
Salty water can’t refreeze at 0°C
Salt lowers water’s freezing point, so ice can melt even when the temperature is around 0°C.

A thin liquid layer exists at the surface of ice. Salt dissolves into that water and lowers its freezing point. At temperatures where pure water would refreeze, the salty solution can remain liquid, so more ice melts to restore equilibrium. Melting absorbs heat from the surroundings, which can make an ice–salt mixture noticeably colder.
FREEZING-POINT DEPRESSION • DISSOLVING • COLLIGATIVE PROPERTIES
H₂O(s) + NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq) (freezing point lowered)
Why does an iron nail left out in the damp turn to orange flakes?
Leave a nail out in the damp. Oil one end and wait.
The air slowly burns it
Water and oxygen together eat into the iron
The metal is simply old and tired
Rust is iron joining with oxygen and water into a crumbly new compound — hydrated iron oxide.

Rusting is an electrochemical corrosion process. Iron is oxidised while oxygen is reduced, and water provides the medium through which ions move. The hydrated iron oxides that form are porous and flaky, so they do not seal the metal from further attack. Paint, oil or other coatings slow rusting by blocking water and oxygen.
OXIDATION • CORROSION • ELECTROCHEMISTRY
4Fe + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·H₂O (rust)
Why does a splash of bleach turn a coloured shirt white?
Drop bleach on a dyed cloth and watch the spot spread.
It rinses the dye out of the fabric
It coats the dye in a layer of white
It breaks the part of the dye that carries colour
Bleach oxidises the dye’s chromophore, changing the bonds that let it absorb visible light.

A dye looks coloured because part of its molecular structure — its chromophore — absorbs particular wavelengths of visible light. Oxidising bleach can disrupt that conjugated structure, so the molecule no longer absorbs the same wavelengths. On a white fabric, the treated area can therefore appear pale or white even though reaction products remain.
OXIDATION • CHROMOPHORES • BOND BREAKING
NaOCl + dye(coloured) → dye(oxidised, colourless) + NaCl
Why does cutting an onion make you cry?
Cut into an onion and watch what rises from the blade.
The smell alone is just very strong
It releases a gas that stings the eyes
Tiny juice droplets splash up into them
Cutting an onion creates a volatile sulfur compound that reaches your eyes and activates irritation nerves.

Cutting breaks onion cells and mixes enzymes with sulfur-containing precursor molecules. Within seconds this chemistry produces syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a volatile lachrymatory factor that drifts into the air. When it reaches the eye’s wet surface it stimulates sensory nerves, and the tear glands respond by flushing the irritant away. Chilling the onion can slow the chemistry and reduce how quickly the vapour is produced.
ENZYMES • SULFUR CHEMISTRY • VOLATILITY
Cysteine sulfoxide → sulfenic acid → syn-propanethial-S-oxide
Why does a splash of vinegar turn milk into lumps?
Stir a spoonful of vinegar into a glass of warm milk.
The milk is freezing into lumps
Acid makes the proteins clump together
The fat rises up and hardens
Acid strips the charge off milk’s proteins, so they stop repelling each other and clump into solid curds.

Milk carries casein proteins as tiny bundles that stay apart because they all hold the same slight negative charge and push one another away. Add acid — from vinegar, or from bacteria as milk sours — and that charge is cancelled. With nothing to keep them apart, the bundles stick together into solid curds and the watery whey separates out. It is the first step in making cheese.
PROTEINS • pH • COLLOIDS
Casein⁻ + CH₃COOH → casein(neutral)↓ + CH₃COO⁻
Why does vinegar strip the chalky crust off a kettle?
Pour vinegar over the crust on an old kettle element.
The vinegar softens it enough to wipe away
The acid reacts with the scale and dissolves it
It just soaks the crust loose over time
Limescale is a mineral base. Vinegar’s acid turns it into things that dissolve — plus a fizz of carbon dioxide.

Hard water bakes calcium carbonate — the same stuff as chalk and limestone — onto the heating element. It will not dissolve in water, but it is a base, and the acetic acid in vinegar reacts with it: the carbonate becomes soluble calcium acetate, water, and carbon dioxide, which bubbles off. The crust simply washes away. Citric acid and lactic acid work the same way.
ACID–BASE • CARBONATES • SOLUBILITY
CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑
Why does a flat bowl of batter climb into a domed cake?
Slide a tin of batter into the oven and watch it climb.
The oven heat puffs up the flour
Gas bubbles form and expand as it bakes
The eggs inflate like balloons
Baking powder releases carbon dioxide into the batter; the oven’s heat expands those bubbles, and the batter sets around them.

Baking powder holds a carbonate and a dry acid side by side. Add liquid and they react, giving off carbon dioxide; the oven’s heat sets off a second burst and expands every bubble already there. The batter is stretchy enough to trap the gas as it grows, and as the starch and egg proteins cook they firm up around the bubbles — locking in a light, open crumb.
ACID–BASE • GAS EXPANSION • DENATURATION
NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑
Why does toothpaste contain fluoride?
Drip acid on two teeth — one plain, one fluoride-treated.
It scrubs the plaque away
It kills the bacteria in your mouth
It helps enamel resist acid and rebuild early mineral loss
Fluoride helps enamel remineralise and makes the repaired surface more resistant to acid attack.

Acids produced by plaque bacteria can dissolve mineral from tooth enamel. Fluoride in saliva and plaque fluid helps shift the balance back toward remineralisation, encouraging calcium and phosphate to redeposit in a more acid-resistant form. It also reduces further demineralisation, which is why frequent low-level fluoride exposure helps prevent cavities.
MINERAL EQUILIBRIA • ACID DISSOLUTION • REMINERALISATION
Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH + F⁻ → Ca₅(PO₄)₃F + OH⁻
Why does perfume fade to nothing within a few hours?
Dab perfume on your skin and follow the scent molecules.
Your nose gets tired of the smell
The scent molecules evaporate and drift away
Your skin absorbs the perfume
The scent molecules are volatile — they escape the drop into the air and spread out until too few reach your nose to smell.

Perfume is a blend of volatile scent molecules, usually carried in alcohol. The alcohol evaporates quickly, followed by the fragrance compounds at different rates according to their vapour pressures and interactions with skin. As those molecules diffuse through the air, their concentration near you falls. Your nose also adapts to a steady odour, so both evaporation and sensory adaptation contribute to the fading experience.
VOLATILITY • VAPOUR PRESSURE • DIFFUSION
Fragrance(l) → fragrance(g)↑ (evaporation)
Why does chilli feel hot when nothing is actually burning you?
Watch what a molecule of capsaicin does to a nerve — and to a thermometer.
Chilli really does raise the temperature in your mouth
It triggers the same nerve sensor that real heat does
It irritates the skin like a scratch
Capsaicin fits the exact nerve receptor that real heat opens — so your brain gets a "burning" signal though nothing is hot.

Nerve endings in the mouth carry the TRPV1 receptor, which normally responds strongly to potentially painful heat. Capsaicin binds to the same receptor and activates it even when the tissue is not actually hot, so the brain receives a burning signal without a matching rise in temperature. Water does little because capsaicin is poorly water-soluble; dairy can help because casein and fat interact with it and help remove it from oral surfaces.
RECEPTOR BINDING • MOLECULAR SHAPE • SIGNALLING
Capsaicin + TRPV1 receptor → “hot” signal (no ΔT)
Why is ice slippery?
Pressure and friction make a microscopic liquid layer.
Pressure and friction create a thin liquid layer on top of the ice
Ice is naturally smooth and hard
Cold surfaces are always slippery
A thin, mobile water layer forms at the ice surface; friction also melts a little more, letting shoes or skates glide.
A thin, mobile water layer forms at the ice surface; friction also melts a little more, letting shoes or skates glide.
surface melting • hydrogen bonding • friction
H₂O(s) → thin H₂O(l) film (pressure + friction)
Why does bread go stale?
Fresh bread slowly loses its soft texture on the counter.
The bread simply dries out completely
Starch molecules re-crystallise and push moisture out of the crumb
Mould is already growing inside
Starch molecules reorganise and crystallise as bread cools, pushing water out of the crumb. This retrogradation makes the loaf firm.
Starch molecules reorganise and crystallise as bread cools, pushing water out of the crumb. This retrogradation makes the loaf firm.
starch • crystallisation • retrogradation
Amylopectin(amorphous) → amylopectin(crystalline) + H₂O
Why do you get static shocks in winter?
A dry jumper crackles, then a metal handle sparks.
Cold air itself carries an electric charge
Synthetic fabric generates a magnetic field
Friction moves electrons, and dry winter air lets the charge build up
Friction transfers electrons between materials. Dry air does not help charge leak away, so the voltage builds until it jumps as a spark.
Friction transfers electrons between materials. Dry air does not help charge leak away, so the voltage builds until it jumps as a spark.
electron transfer • charge • humidity
A + B → A⁺ + B⁻ (friction) → spark discharge
Why do bananas turn brown?
A green banana softens, sweetens, then its peel darkens.
Ripening enzymes oxidise the peel’s compounds into dark pigments
The peel is simply bruised by handling
Sunlight darkens the skin

Ripening enzymes break cell walls and convert starch to sugar. Oxidation of phenolic compounds then produces dark pigments in the peel.

Phenolics + O₂ → o-quinones → melanin

The knife leaves a metal residue that stains it
Oxygen reacts with enzyme-exposed compounds in the cut flesh
The avocado is simply overripe

Cutting ruptures cells, mixing polyphenol oxidase with oxygen and phenols. The enzyme-driven oxidation makes brown quinone pigments.

Why does lemon taste sour?
A squeeze of lemon makes your mouth react instantly.
Lemon is naturally bitter, which we read as sour
The lemon’s sugar reacts with saliva
Citric acid releases hydrogen ions that taste receptors detect
Citric acid releases hydrogen ions in saliva. Taste receptors detect the acidity, while the buffer system in your mouth begins neutralising it.
Citric acid releases hydrogen ions in saliva. Taste receptors detect the acidity, while the buffer system in your mouth begins neutralising it.

Why does baking soda fizz with vinegar?
Two kitchen powders and liquids suddenly produce bubbles.
Acid and bicarbonate react and release carbon dioxide gas
The two liquids heat up and start to boil
Air trapped in the powder escapes
Acetic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate to form carbon dioxide, water and sodium acetate. The escaping CO₂ makes the fizz.
Acetic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate to form carbon dioxide, water and sodium acetate. The escaping CO₂ makes the fizz.

NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂↑

A dry powder becomes bubbles when batter is heated.
The oven’s heat expands trapped air alone
An acid and a bicarbonate react and release carbon dioxide as it bakes
The flour simply swells as it absorbs water
Acid and bicarbonate in baking powder react in moist batter, releasing CO₂. Heat expands the bubbles while proteins and starch set the crumb.
Acid and bicarbonate in baking powder react in moist batter, releasing CO₂. Heat expands the bubbles while proteins and starch set the crumb.

NaHCO₃ + H⁺ → Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑
Why does yeast make dough rise?
A quiet dough doubles in size before baking.
Yeast heats the dough from the inside
Kneading pumps air into the dough
Yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide, trapped by the gluten
Yeast metabolises sugars without oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and ethanol. Gluten traps the gas in stretchy pockets.
Yeast metabolises sugars without oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and ethanol. Gluten traps the gas in stretchy pockets.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂↑
How does milk become yogurt?
Warm milk turns tangy and thick after a day.
Bacteria turn milk sugar into acid, which curdles the proteins
The milk simply cools and thickens
Warm milk naturally separates over time

Bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid. Lower pH changes casein interactions, forming a soft protein gel.

How does milk become cheese?
Milk separates into curds and whey in a vat.
The milk fat rises and solidifies
Acid or rennet makes the milk proteins clump into curds
Cheese forms wherever milk is left out too long

Acid or rennet makes casein proteins aggregate into curds. Pressing removes whey and concentrates the fat and protein.

Why does egg white turn white when cooked?
Clear egg white becomes firm and opaque in a pan.
The egg white loses water and shrinks
Cooking bleaches the egg white
Heat unfolds the proteins into a network that scatters light
Heat unfolds albumin proteins. The unfolded chains link into a network that scatters light and traps water.
Heat unfolds albumin proteins. The unfolded chains link into a network that scatters light and traps water.

A runny yolk becomes creamy, then solid.
Heat unfolds yolk proteins into a firmer network
The fat in the yolk melts and resolidifies
The yolk simply loses moisture

Heat denatures yolk proteins and changes the emulsion. Continued heating creates a tighter protein network and a firmer gel.

Anthocyanin pigments change structure as pH changes, shifting which wavelengths of light they absorb.

Tea tannins and pigments respond to acidity. Lower pH changes their molecular form and therefore their colour.
